title: Collaborative Drug Therapy Management: What It Is, Who May Do It, Where, and For Whom
topic: Collaborative practice / Entry conditions for collaborative drug therapy management
subtopic: The statutory definition and its diagnostic boundary; the pharmacist qualification elements as M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b), 247 CMR 16.02(1) and 243 CMR 2.12(2) each state them, together with the definition of an Authorized Pharmacist in 243 CMR 2.12(1); the four settings in § 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4) and their approving bodies; the employment relationships permitted and prohibited by § 24B1/2(e) and 247 CMR 16.04(7); supervising-physician qualifications and ineligibility under 243 CMR 2.12(3); the definition of a collaborative patient; and the two meanings of Referral in 243 CMR 2.12(1)
learning_objectives: State the four core verbs of the statutory definition of collaborative drug therapy management and distinguish them from the activities the definition merely may include.
Apply the three conditions attached to the laboratory limb and locate the diagnostic boundary that limits what an evaluation may conclude.
Run a pharmacist's facts against the qualification elements as each of the three instruments states them, and say where 247 CMR 16.02(1) is narrower than M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b).
Decide whether the credential element is satisfied by reading 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) and its two subparagraphs, including what the June 30, 2017 date does to the doctor of pharmacy route.

State the licence, insurance and continuing-education elements in the words the regulations use, including unrestricted and in good standing, per occurrence, and cover specific to drug therapy management.
Explain why 247 CMR 16.02 governs a pharmacist even when a question is framed on the Board of Registration in Medicine's regulation.
Name the approving body for each of the four settings in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4) without carrying one setting's approval across to another.
Identify the additional on-site supervision condition unique to the ambulatory care clinic setting and treat it as cumulative with approval.
Decide whether a proposed employment arrangement is permitted by asking which way the hiring runs and for what purpose, and separate the quality-assurance carve-out from the prohibited purpose.

State what makes a physician eligible to participate under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a), and determine when a supervising physician has become ineligible under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d), including on a controlled substances registration event alone, and explain why the absence of notice proves nothing.
Apply the statutory definition of patient, including the physician's assessment and diagnosis, the setting-specific notice and consent, and the recording duty that binds both professionals.

Give the two meanings of Referral in 243 CMR 2.12(1), list the contents a community-pharmacy written referral shall include, and keep that definition separate from the physician's duty under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) to assess the patient and make a written referral.

orientation.text: Collaborative drug therapy management is defined in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) as the initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing of a patient's drug therapy by a pharmacist in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement. Those four verbs are the whole of the core definition, and each of them operates only through the agreement. The definition then adds three things the practice may include, and they are not equally conditioned. Collecting and reviewing patient histories, and obtaining and checking vital signs including pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration, are stated without any attached condition. The laboratory limb is stated with three conditions at once: the pharmacist acts under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician; the work is performed in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting; and the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component. The last of those is the boundary of the whole authority. Satisfying the conditions for ordering a test does nothing to enlarge what the pharmacist's evaluation of the result may conclude, so a properly ordered test does not license a diagnosis drawn from it.

Who may collaborate is settled before any of that, and it is settled by three instruments that do not say the same thing. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) lists six things a pharmacist shall do or have in order to enter into a collaborative practice agreement. The pharmacist shall hold a current licence to practise pharmacy in the commonwealth and currently be engaged in pharmacy practice in the commonwealth, which is two requirements in one clause and not one. The pharmacist shall have at least 1,000,000 dollars of professional liability insurance. The pharmacist shall have earned a doctor of pharmacy degree or have completed five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist or the equivalent, which the statute states as alternatives rather than cumulatively. The pharmacist shall agree to devote a portion of practice to the defined drug therapy area to be co-managed, and shall agree to complete, in each year of the agreement, at least five additional contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units of board-approved continuing education addressing areas of practice generally related to collaborative practice agreements. The sixth element is conditional rather than absolute: the pharmacist shall apply to participate in the medical assistance program for the limited purpose of ordering and referring covered services if regulations governing that limited participation are promulgated under chapter 118E. Answer a question framed on the statute from those words, but do not stop there, because a pharmacist who is actually going to practise has to satisfy the regulations as well, and neither 247 CMR 16.02(1) nor 243 CMR 2.12(2) stops where the statute does.

247 CMR 16.02(1) is the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's version of the same list, and it governs a pharmacist who wants to qualify to enter into a collaborative practice agreement and engage in collaborative practice. Its licence element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(a), is a current unrestricted license in good standing to practice pharmacy in the Commonwealth together with current engagement in Massachusetts pharmacy practice, so a pharmacist practising under a live restriction fails it while holding a licence that is perfectly current. Its insurance element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b), is at least $1,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance, maintained during the term of the agreement, which specifically covers drug therapy management; an aggregate-only policy, a policy that lapses mid-term and a general pharmacist policy that does not reach drug therapy management each fail it with the right figure on the page. The credential element is the one that decides fact patterns. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) requires five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist unless the pharmacist has satisfied one of the requirements in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. through 2. Subparagraph 1. is a doctor of pharmacy degree and a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, both limbs together. Subparagraph 2. is such other education or residency criteria as the Board determines to be the equivalent of five years experience. So a pharmacist entering an agreement today cannot reach the element on the degree alone: that route is closed by its own date, and what is left is the five years or a Board determination of equivalence. The continuing-education element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e), is five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term, with no continuing education unit alternative stated, addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular collaborative practice agreement. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(f) adds further conditions, but only where prescriptive practices are included in the agreement, and those belong to the separate section on prescribing.

It would be a mistake to treat 247 CMR 16.02 as the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's private business. 243 CMR 2.12(1) defines an Authorized Pharmacist as a pharmacist who is currently registered by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and is in good standing, who meets the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02, and who is participating in drug therapy management with a supervising physician pursuant to a written agreement with written protocols. The three limbs are stated together, so a pharmacist who does not meet 247 CMR 16.02 is not an authorized pharmacist for the Board of Registration in Medicine's purposes either. That board nevertheless keeps its own qualification list, and it is not identical. 243 CMR 2.12(2)(a) and (b) state the licence and insurance elements in the same words the pharmacy regulation uses. But 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) states the credential element as the statute does, a doctor of pharmacy degree or five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist, with no date attached to the degree; and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e) keeps the five contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units alternative while tying the subject matter, as the pharmacy regulation does, to the particular agreement. When a question gives you a pharmacist who holds the degree but not the years, read which instrument the question is asking about: the statute and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) are answered by the degree alone, and 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) is not. For a pharmacist actually proposing to practise, the narrower provision is the operative one, because 243 CMR 2.12(1) makes meeting 247 CMR 16.02 part of what it is to be an authorized pharmacist.

Where collaborative practice may happen is a closed list with a different approving body attached to each entry, and the single most common error in this area is to carry one approval across all of them. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4), a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51 requires approval by the medical staff executive committee at the licensed hospital or a designee; a long-term care facility licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 71 requires approval by the facility's medical director or a designee; an inpatient or outpatient hospice setting licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 57D requires approval by the hospice's medical director or a designee; and an ambulatory care clinic requires approval by the clinic's medical staff executive committee or designee, or its medical director or designee. The ambulatory care clinic carries a condition none of the other three does, and it is cumulative with approval rather than an alternative to it: collaborative practice there is allowed with on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist. Note also that the hospital limb and the ambulatory care clinic limb both rest on the same licensing provision, M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, so a difference in licensing section is not what separates them. These four limbs are the ones this section teaches; collaborative practice by a pharmacist in a retail drug business is dealt with by a separate section.

Employment is regulated by purpose, not by the bare fact of a hiring, and the direction of the hiring matters. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(e) permits a physician or a physician group to hire pharmacists for the purpose of practising collaborative drug therapy management under an agreement for the benefit of a patient of that physician or physician group. Running the same arrangement the other way is where the bar falls: no retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement with a patient. The same subsection then preserves an engagement that looks superficially similar, providing that nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy. The implementing regulation, 247 CMR 16.04(7), states the same three propositions in its own order -- the permission at (a), the quality-assurance saving at (b) and the prohibition at (c) -- with one difference of vocabulary worth noticing: where the statute says retail pharmacy, 247 CMR 16.04(7)(b) and (c) say community pharmacy. The two instruments are describing the same setting under different labels, so a fact pattern that uses either word is asking about the same rule. One further difference of wording is worth noting rather than worrying about: the statute closes its prohibition with the words with a patient and 247 CMR 16.04(7)(c) does not, but both turn on the purpose of the employment rather than on the fact of it.

Before asking whether a supervising physician has become ineligible, ask what made him eligible in the first place, because the regulation states a positive requirement and not merely a list of disqualifications. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a) a physician must possess an active license to practice medicine issued by the Board and must be actively engaged in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field of medicine in which the collaborative drug therapy management is to take place. That is two things again, and the second is field-specific: a licensed physician who has left clinical practice, or who is in active practice but in a different field from the therapy to be co-managed, does not satisfy it. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(b) then fixes the relationship. The physician is the supervisor in the agreement and retains the ultimate responsibility for the care of the patient, and in a community pharmacy setting a physician should enter into only as many agreements as he or she can reasonably and safely supervise at one time. And 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) puts a documentary duty on the physician: the supervising physician shall assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient to the authorized pharmacist, and that written referral shall include a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions that are included in the collaborative management. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) states that duty without confining it to one practice setting, which is worth holding beside the setting-sensitive definition of Referral taken up further below.

A collaboration can also fail from the physician's side, and it can fail silently. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) a physician is ineligible to participate in collaborative drug therapy management if he or she is in a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine with the Board, or has had a licence to practise medicine temporarily suspended or revoked by the Board. Separately, a physician shall be deemed ineligible if he or she has voluntarily surrendered, or has had suspended, revoked or restricted, a controlled substances licence, permit or registration, either state or federal. That second sentence is the one that catches people out, because it turns on a registration rather than on the medical licence, it reaches a federal event as readily as a state one, and it reaches a mere restriction as well as a surrender or revocation. The same provision allows the Board to revoke a physician's right to participate in a collaborative agreement on any of the grounds for discipline in 243 CMR 1.03(5). Notice is not the trigger. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(e), where the Board enters into a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice with a licensee, summarily suspends a licence, or takes final disciplinary action by final decision and order or by approving a consent agreement, the Board may require the physician to give written notification to each authorized pharmacist with whom he or she is in an agreement. That is a discretion, so the absence of notice tells the pharmacist nothing about whether the authority still exists.

Eligibility of the patient is a separate gate, and it sits upstream of every clinical act. The definition of patient in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) is a person who is referred to a pharmacist by his supervising physician for the purpose of receiving collaborative drug therapy management services from the pharmacist. A person who asks for the service, or who reports that a physician mentioned it, is not yet a patient within the definition. The definition then loads three further duties onto that one sentence. The supervising physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist, so a referral carrying no diagnosis is incomplete on its face. The patient shall be notified of, and shall consent to, the services in the retail drug business setting, which is a setting-specific requirement rather than a universal one. And individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record, which binds both professionals; an entry made by the physician alone does not discharge the pharmacist's duty, and an entry made by the pharmacist alone does not discharge the physician's.

The word referral does not mean the same thing everywhere, and this is the point at which identical facts produce opposite answers in two settings. Under 243 CMR 2.12(1), Referral means the individual patient referral by a supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist for the purpose of receiving collaborative services in a community pharmacy setting; in all other practice settings, Referral means the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist about a patient for that purpose. So a conversation between a physician and a pharmacist about a named patient can itself be the referral in a hospital, a long-term care facility, a hospice or an ambulatory care clinic, while the same conversation in a community pharmacy is not one. In the community pharmacy setting the supervising physician shall execute a written referral, and 243 CMR 2.12(1) lists what it shall include without limiting it to those items: the patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis for which the services are authorized, the diagnosis of any comorbid conditions for which they are authorized, any known patient drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent, and any other specific instructions to the authorized pharmacist. Two of the named items are easy to leave out, the allergies and the statement about consent, and a referral that is signed, detailed and specific is still incomplete without them. Keep the definition separate from the physician's own duty: 243 CMR 2.12(1) tells you what counts as a Referral in each setting, while 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) separately requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management, and states that duty without a setting limit. So a consultation in a hospital is a Referral within the definition without discharging the physician's own writing duty.

It is worth fixing what this section does not reach, because collaborative practice is split across several sections and the boundaries are drawn by subject rather than by instrument. This section covers the entry conditions only: what collaborative drug therapy management is and where its diagnostic boundary falls, which pharmacists qualify under the statute and under each board's regulation, which settings allow the practice and who approves it in each, who may employ whom, what makes a supervising physician eligible and when he stops being eligible, who counts as a patient, and what a referral is in each setting. What the collaborative practice agreement itself must contain, how it is renewed, filed, delegated under and terminated, is the subject of a separate section. What a pharmacist may actually prescribe, modify or discontinue once the agreement is in place is the subject of another. The distinct regime that governs the retail drug business setting, including its own scope limits on patients, diseases and drug therapy, is the subject of a third. When a question turns on any of those, the answer is not in the material below, and reasoning from the entry conditions to a conclusion about agreement terms or prescribing powers is the wrong move.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborating pharmacist in a licensed hospital reviews a co-managed patient's history, then takes her pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration at the bedside. Her unit has no approved protocol covering laboratory work and the supervising physician is off site and unreachable, so she orders a serum potassium herself because the therapy she manages plainly calls for one. Which of the two acts is inside the definition?
steps: Take the history first. Collecting and reviewing patient histories is a stated may-include limb of M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a), and the definition attaches no condition to it.

Take the vital signs next. Obtaining and checking vital signs, including pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration, is a separate stated limb and it too carries no physician-involvement or protocol condition.

Now read the laboratory limb, which is conditioned three ways: under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician; in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting; and with an evaluation that shall not include a diagnostic component.
Two of those three conditions fail here on the facts, because there is no approved protocol for the setting and no supervision or direct consultation at the time of ordering.
worked_examples.resolution: The history and the vital signs are within collaborative drug therapy management; the laboratory order is not. The error the scenario invites is treating the three may-include limbs as equally conditioned and inferring that whatever is clinically sensible for the managed therapy must be authorised.

worked_examples.scenario: An ambulatory care clinic licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51 has approval from its medical staff executive committee for collaborative drug therapy management. The collaborating pharmacist works in the clinic itself, but the attending physician covers three sites and is present by video link only, never in the building. The clinic manager argues that the approval requirement has been satisfied and that nothing else in the settings list is left to meet.
steps: Identify the setting and the approving body. For an ambulatory care clinic, M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(4) accepts approval by the clinic's medical staff executive committee or designee, or by its medical director or designee, so the approval here is from a correct body.
Read the rest of the same limb. It permits collaborative practice in that setting with on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist.
Treat the two elements as cumulative rather than alternative, because the limb states approval and on-site supervision together and no other setting in the list carries the supervision condition.
Apply that to the facts: the pharmacist is on site but the attending physician is not, so the on-site supervision element is unmet however sound the approval is.
worked_examples.resolution: The arrangement does not comply, because approval and on-site supervision by the attending physician are both required in an ambulatory care clinic. The error the scenario invites is reading approval by the right body as the whole of the setting requirement.

worked_examples.scenario: A retail pharmacy chain puts two physicians under contract. The first is retained, under a contract titled medical director for collaborative practice, to negotiate and sign collaborative practice agreements covering the chain's collaborating pharmacists. The second is retained to audit a sample of co-managed patient charts each quarter and report on the quality of the pharmacists' collaborative work. The chain treats both as ordinary professional services contracts.
steps: Ask what each engagement is for, because M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(e) turns on the purpose of the employment and not on the fact of it or on the job title used.

Test the first engagement against the prohibition: no retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement, and negotiating and signing agreements is precisely that purpose.

Test the second against the preserved engagement: nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy.

Check the implementing regulation for the same result: 247 CMR 16.04(7)(b) permits the quality assurance engagement and 247 CMR 16.04(7)(c) bars the agreement engagement, using the label community pharmacy for the same setting.
worked_examples.resolution: The chart-audit engagement is permitted and the agreement-signing engagement is prohibited. The error the scenario invites is reading the subsection as a blanket bar on a pharmacy employing any physician, or as satisfied by a job title that describes the prohibited purpose in quality-assurance language.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborating pharmacist is told by a colleague that her supervising physician's state controlled substances registration was restricted last week following a settlement. The physician's licence to practise medicine is active and unrestricted, he is not in any Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine, and neither board has sent the pharmacist anything. She has a full clinic of co-managed patients booked for the afternoon.
steps: Separate the two sentences of 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d). The first turns on the medical licence and on a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine; the second turns on a controlled substances licence, permit or registration.

Apply the second sentence, which deems a physician ineligible where such a registration has been voluntarily surrendered, or has been suspended, revoked or restricted, either state or federal; a restriction counts, and the state or federal character makes no difference.
Do not let the intact medical licence rescue the collaboration, because the second sentence operates independently of the first.

Do not treat the absence of notice as evidence, because 243 CMR 2.12(3)(e) makes notification something the Board may require on the events it lists, and a controlled substances registration event is not among those events.
worked_examples.resolution: The physician is deemed ineligible and the collaboration cannot continue that afternoon. The error the scenario invites is reasoning from an unrestricted medical licence, or from having heard nothing from any board, to the conclusion that the authority survives.

worked_examples.scenario: On the same day, a hospital pharmacist and a community pharmacist each speak to a supervising physician about a named patient and each begins collaborative management on the strength of that conversation. Two days later the community pharmacist receives a signed written referral giving the patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis, one authorized comorbid diagnosis and detailed instructions, but silent on allergies and on consent. Both pharmacists note the referral in their own records only.
steps: Apply the setting-sensitive definition in 243 CMR 2.12(1): in all practice settings other than a community pharmacy, Referral means the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist about a patient for the purpose of the patient's receiving the services, so the hospital conversation is itself a referral.

Apply the community pharmacy branch of the same definition: there, Referral means the individual patient referral and the supervising physician shall execute a written referral, so the identical conversation is not a referral in that setting.

Measure the written referral against the contents listed in 243 CMR 2.12(1), which include any known patient drug allergies and a statement that the patient has executed a written consent; both are missing, so the document is incomplete despite being signed and detailed.

Read the patient definition in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) for the recording duty: individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record, so a note made by one professional alone leaves the other's duty undischarged.

Keep the physician's own duty separate from the definition. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management, and it is not confined to one setting, so the hospital consultation satisfies the definition of Referral without discharging that duty.
worked_examples.resolution: The hospital pharmacist was properly referred within the meaning of Referral and the community pharmacist was not, neither recording is sufficient on its own, and in both settings the supervising physician still owes the assess-and-write duty in 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c). The error the scenario invites is assuming that one meaning of referral governs every setting, that whichever professional writes the note discharges the duty for both, and that the definition disposes of the physician's separate obligation.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist proposes to enter a collaborative practice agreement this year. She holds a current Massachusetts pharmacist licence, subject to a Board-imposed restriction that is still in force; she has worked exclusively as a medical science liaison for the last three years; she carries a 1,000,000 dollar aggregate professional liability policy covering general pharmacy practice; she earned a doctor of pharmacy degree in 2019; she will co-manage hypertension; and she plans to complete her five additional collaborative-practice contact hours once at the start of the agreement rather than in each year of it.
steps: Start with the statute, because a question framed on M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) is asking about the statute: a current licence together with current engagement in Massachusetts practice, at least 1,000,000 dollars of professional liability insurance, a doctor of pharmacy degree or five years of experience or the equivalent, the practice-focus agreement, the annual continuing education, and the conditional medical assistance application.

Then read 247 CMR 16.02(1), which she must satisfy to qualify to enter an agreement and engage in collaborative practice. Its licence element is a current unrestricted license in good standing, so the live restriction defeats it even though the licence is current, and the second half of the element, current engagement in Massachusetts pharmacy practice, is doubtful on three years as a medical science liaison.

Test the insurance against the words of 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) rather than against the figure alone: at least $1,000,000 per occurrence, maintained during the term of the agreement, specifically covering drug therapy management. An aggregate limit is not a per-occurrence limit, and a general pharmacy policy is not cover that specifically reaches drug therapy management, so she fails on cover twice over with the right number on the page.

Run the credential element through 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c). Five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist is the standard, and the alternatives are 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1., a doctor of pharmacy degree together with a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, and 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)2., other education or residency criteria the Board determines to be equivalent. Her degree is from 2019 and the agreement is being entered now, so the first alternative is unavailable and nothing in the facts engages the second.

Finish with the continuing education. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) requires five additional contact hours in each year of the term addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular agreement, so a single front-loaded block does not carry a multi-year agreement; and the contact-hours-or-0.5-units choice she may have in mind comes from the statute and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e), not from the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's regulation.
worked_examples.resolution: She does not qualify under 247 CMR 16.02(1): the restriction defeats the licence element, the policy is neither per occurrence nor specific to drug therapy management, the credential element is unmet because the doctor of pharmacy route in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. reaches only an agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, and the continuing education has to recur in each year of the term. Her current engagement in Massachusetts pharmacy practice also has to be established. The error the scenario invites is answering from the statute alone and treating the doctor of pharmacy degree as an element-ending fact, when the regulation she must satisfy gives the degree work to do only in combination with an agreement entered on or before that date.

worked_examples.scenario: A dermatologist in active hospital practice proposes to become the supervising physician for a collaborating pharmacist who will co-manage anticoagulation on a medical ward. His licence to practise medicine is active and unrestricted, he is in no Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine, his controlled substances registrations are intact, and the hospital's medical staff executive committee has approved collaborative drug therapy management. He asks whether anything stands in the way.
steps: Take the approval question first, because it is the one people answer. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(1) a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51 requires approval by the medical staff executive committee at the licensed hospital or a designee, and that approval is in place.

Now read the positive requirement in 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a): an active license to practice medicine issued by the Board, and active engagement in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field of medicine in which the collaborative drug therapy management is to take place.

Separate the two halves. The licence half is satisfied on these facts. The practice half asks about the particular field, and the field in which he is actively engaged is dermatology while the proposed collaboration is anticoagulation management on a medical ward.

Check the ineligibility provision as well, so that the answer does not come to rest on it by mistake. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) turns on a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine, a temporary suspension or revocation of the medical licence, or a controlled substances licence, permit or registration that has been surrendered, suspended, revoked or restricted; none of those is in the facts.
worked_examples.resolution: Nothing in 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) disqualifies him, and the setting has been approved by the right body, but he does not satisfy 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a), because the field in which he is actively engaged is not the field of the proposed collaboration. The error the scenario invites is treating eligibility as the absence of a disqualifying event, when the provision states a positive requirement that is field-specific.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four verbs at the core of the statutory definition of collaborative drug therapy management.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing a patient's drug therapy, in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement, under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The laboratory limb of the definition carries three conditions. What are they?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician; performed in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting; and the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because the vital-signs limb and the laboratory limb sit in the same sentence, both need physician involvement.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Only the laboratory limb is conditioned on physician supervision or direct consultation and on approved protocols; obtaining and checking vital signs is stated without those conditions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the insurance element as 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) states it, not just the figure.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Maintain at least $1,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance during the term of the agreement, and the cover must specifically cover drug therapy management. 243 CMR 2.12(2)(b) requires an agreement to maintain the same cover; M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) states the figure alone.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How much additional continuing education does a collaborating pharmacist take on, how often, and where do the three instruments differ?
retrieval_prompts.answer: In each year of the agreement term. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) states at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular agreement, with no continuing education unit alternative. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e) state five contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units, and the statute describes the subject matter as generally related to collaborative practice agreements rather than to the particular one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist with a doctor of pharmacy degree and two years of licensed experience wants to enter a collaborative practice agreement this year. Does the degree satisfy 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) requires five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist unless one of the requirements in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. through 2. is satisfied, and subparagraph 1. requires the degree together with a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017. Subparagraph 2. is open only on a Board determination that other education or residency criteria are the equivalent of five years experience.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) state the credential element, how does 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c), and which governs a pharmacist who is proposing to practise?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute states a doctor of pharmacy degree, or five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist, or the equivalent, as alternatives. 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) states a doctor of pharmacy degree or five years of experience, with no date attached. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) is the narrower one, and 243 CMR 2.12(1) makes meeting 247 CMR 16.02 part of the definition of an authorized pharmacist, so the narrower provision is the operative one for a pharmacist proposing to practise.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the licence element in the words both regulations use.
retrieval_prompts.answer: A current unrestricted license in good standing to practice pharmacy in the Commonwealth, together with current engagement in pharmacy practice in the Commonwealth. See 247 CMR 16.02(1)(a) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the three limbs of the definition of Authorized Pharmacist in 243 CMR 2.12(1)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Currently registered by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and in good standing; meets the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02; and is participating in drug therapy management with a supervising physician pursuant to a written agreement with written protocols.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which qualification element in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) applies only on a condition, and what is that condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The application to participate in the medical assistance program for the limited purpose of ordering and referring covered services, which bites if regulations governing that limited participation are promulgated under chapter 118E.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Match the approving body to the setting: hospital, long-term care facility, hospice, ambulatory care clinic.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Hospital, the medical staff executive committee at the licensed hospital or designee; long-term care facility, the facility's medical director or designee; hospice, the hospice's medical director or designee; ambulatory care clinic, the clinic's medical staff executive committee or designee, or its medical director or designee.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which of the four listed settings carries a condition beyond approval, and what is it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The ambulatory care clinic, which requires on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist in addition to approval.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A retail pharmacy wants to put a physician on its payroll. When is that lawful and when is it not?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Lawful for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists engaged in collaborative drug therapy; unlawful for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement. See M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(e) and 247 CMR 16.04(7).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A supervising physician keeps an unrestricted medical licence but has had his federal controlled substances registration restricted. Is he eligible?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. He is deemed ineligible under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d), which reaches a controlled substances licence, permit or registration that is surrendered, suspended, revoked or restricted, either state or federal.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who must record the individual referral and consent, and where?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Both the pharmacist and the supervising physician, in the patient's record, under the definition of patient in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Referral means ______ in a community pharmacy setting, and ______ in all other practice settings.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the individual patient referral by a supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist; the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist about a patient for that purpose. See 243 CMR 2.12(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the items a written community-pharmacy referral shall include under 243 CMR 2.12(1).
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis for which the services are authorized, the diagnosis of any comorbid conditions for which they are authorized, any known patient drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent, and any other specific instructions to the authorized pharmacist; the list is expressly not exhaustive.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In which setting does the statutory patient definition require notice and consent?
retrieval_prompts.answer: In the retail drug business setting; the definition in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) states the notice and consent requirement for that setting rather than for every setting.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What makes a physician eligible to participate under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a), and what does 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) require of him?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An active license to practice medicine issued by the Board, and active engagement in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field of medicine in which the collaborative drug therapy management is to take place. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) requires him to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient, including a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management.

quick_review.text: Collaborative drug therapy management is the initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing of a patient's drug therapy by a pharmacist in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement, under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a).

The definition may also include collecting and reviewing patient histories and obtaining and checking vital signs, including pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration, with no further condition attached to either limb.

Ordering and evaluating laboratory tests is permitted only under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician, in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting, and when the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component.

M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) requires a current Massachusetts pharmacist licence together with current engagement in pharmacy practice in the commonwealth; 247 CMR 16.02(1)(a) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(a) require that licence to be current, unrestricted and in good standing.

The insurance element is at least $1,000,000 per occurrence under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(b), maintained during the term of the agreement and specifically covering drug therapy management; M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) states the figure without those qualifications.

247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) requires five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist unless the pharmacist satisfies 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1., a doctor of pharmacy degree together with a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, or 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)2., other education or residency criteria the Board determines to be the equivalent of five years experience.

M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) state a doctor of pharmacy degree as a free-standing alternative to five years of experience; 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) does not, and 243 CMR 2.12(1) makes meeting 247 CMR 16.02 part of being an authorized pharmacist.

The continuing-education element recurs in each year of the agreement term: five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e), or five contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e).

Collaborative practice is allowed in hospitals licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, long-term care facilities licensed under § 71, inpatient or outpatient hospice settings licensed under § 57D, and ambulatory care clinics licensed under § 51, each with its own approving body.
Only the ambulatory care clinic limb adds on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist, and that condition sits alongside approval rather than replacing it.
A physician or physician group may hire pharmacists to practise collaborative drug therapy management under an agreement for the benefit of a patient of that physician or group.

No retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement, and 247 CMR 16.04(7)(c) states the same bar for a community pharmacy.

A physician is ineligible under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) while in a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine with the Board, or where the licence to practise medicine has been temporarily suspended or revoked by the Board.
A physician is deemed ineligible where a controlled substances licence, permit or registration has been voluntarily surrendered or has been suspended, revoked or restricted, either state or federal.
A patient is a person referred to a pharmacist by his supervising physician for the purpose of receiving the services; the physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring.
Individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record; the duty binds both professionals.

Under 243 CMR 2.12(1), Referral means the individual patient referral in a community pharmacy setting and the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist in all other practice settings.

A community-pharmacy written referral shall include the patient's name and address, the primary and authorized comorbid diagnoses, any known drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent, and any other specific instructions.

243 CMR 2.12(3)(a) makes a physician eligible only if he holds an active licence to practise medicine issued by the Board and is actively engaged in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field in which the collaborative management is to take place; 243 CMR 2.12(3)(b) makes him the supervisor who retains ultimate responsibility for the care of the patient.

243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management, and states that duty without limiting it to one setting.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist asks whether a proposed activity is inside collaborative drug therapy management.
decision_logic.action: Place the activity against M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a): if it is initiating, monitoring, modifying or discontinuing drug therapy it is core; if it is history-taking or vital signs it is a stated may-include limb with no attached condition; if it is laboratory work run the three conditions; if it is a diagnostic conclusion it is outside.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist has ordered a laboratory test correctly and is now reading the result.
decision_logic.action: Stop at the diagnostic boundary. The evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component, and nothing about a correctly satisfied ordering condition enlarges what the evaluation may conclude.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist wants to know whether she may enter a collaborative practice agreement at all.
decision_logic.action: Run the elements through all three instruments rather than one. Take M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) for a question framed on the statute; then run 247 CMR 16.02(1), which she must satisfy to qualify to enter an agreement and engage in collaborative practice and which 243 CMR 2.12(1) folds into the definition of an authorized pharmacist; then check 243 CMR 2.12(2) where the question is framed on the Board of Registration in Medicine's regulation. Remember that the licence element has two halves and that both regulations require the licence to be unrestricted and in good standing, that the insurance is per occurrence, held for the term and specific to drug therapy management, that 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) closes the doctor of pharmacy route to agreements entered after June 30, 2017, that the continuing education recurs in each year of the term, and that the statutory medical assistance element is conditional on regulations being promulgated under chapter 118E.

decision_logic.condition: The facts give a pharmacist a doctor of pharmacy degree and ask whether the credential element is met.
decision_logic.action: Ask when the collaborative practice agreement was entered. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. couples the degree with an agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, so for an agreement entered after that date the element has to be met by five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist or by a Board determination under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)2. If the question is expressly about M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) or 243 CMR 2.12(2), answer on that instrument's own words.

decision_logic.condition: A physician is proposed as the supervising physician.
decision_logic.action: Check 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a) for eligibility before checking 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) for ineligibility. The physician needs an active licence to practise medicine issued by the Board and active engagement in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field in which the collaborative management will take place, so the absence of any disqualifying event does not by itself make him eligible.

decision_logic.condition: A facility asks who has to sign off on collaborative practice there.
decision_logic.action: Identify the setting first, then read the approving body off M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4) for that setting alone; never carry one setting's approval across to another, and never assume a single system-wide approval covers several settings.

decision_logic.condition: The setting is an ambulatory care clinic.
decision_logic.action: Check approval and on-site supervision as two separate requirements, because that limb permits collaborative practice with on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist in addition to approval.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy or physician group proposes to employ the other profession.
decision_logic.action: Ask which way the hiring runs and what its purpose is. A physician or physician group hiring pharmacists to practise collaborative drug therapy management is permitted; a retail or community pharmacy employing a physician to maintain, establish or enter into an agreement is prohibited; the same pharmacy hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for quality assurance reviews is preserved.

decision_logic.condition: Something has happened to the supervising physician's licence or registration.
decision_logic.action: Read 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) in two parts: a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine or a temporary suspension or revocation of the medical licence makes the physician ineligible; any surrender, suspension, revocation or restriction of a controlled substances licence, permit or registration, state or federal, deems the physician ineligible on its own.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist has received no notice from any board and wants to rely on that silence.
decision_logic.action: Do not. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(e) the Board may require the physician to notify each authorized pharmacist on the events it lists, so silence is consistent with the authority having ended.

Confirm that the supervising physician referred the person for the purpose of receiving the services, that the physician assessed the person and included a diagnosis in the referral, and, in the retail drug business setting, that the person was notified of and consented to the services.

decision_logic.condition: The referral and consent have to be documented.
decision_logic.action: Record them in the patient's record, and confirm that both the pharmacist and the supervising physician have done so, because the duty is stated as binding both.

decision_logic.condition: You need to know whether a referral has actually happened.
decision_logic.action: Identify the setting before reading the facts. In a community pharmacy look for the supervising physician's executed written referral with the contents listed in 243 CMR 2.12(1); in every other practice setting a consultation of the supervising physician and the authorized pharmacist about the patient is itself the referral.

exceptions.text: The prohibition on a retail pharmacy employing a physician has an express carve-out: nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy, and 247 CMR 16.04(7)(b) states the same permission.

The doctor of pharmacy route in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. is itself conditional: it requires the degree and a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)2. leaves a second route open on a Board determination that other education or residency criteria are the equivalent of five years experience.
The 0.5 continuing education unit alternative appears in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e); 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) states the five contact hours alone.

The sixth qualification element is conditional rather than absolute: the duty to apply for limited medical assistance participation for ordering and referring covered services applies if regulations governing such limited participation are promulgated under chapter 118E.
Notice and consent are stated for the retail drug business setting in the definition of patient, not as a universal condition of every collaborative setting.

The written referral formalities are the community pharmacy exception to the ordinary meaning of referral; in all other practice settings a consultation between the supervising physician and the authorized pharmacist about the patient satisfies the definition.

timing_deadlines.event: Additional continuing education undertaken by a collaborating pharmacist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: In each year of the term of the agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) requires at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular agreement in each year of the term, and M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e) state five contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units on the same annual cadence, so a single block completed once does not carry a multi-year agreement.

timing_deadlines.event: Professional liability insurance held by a collaborating pharmacist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: During the term of the agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(b) require the $1,000,000 per occurrence cover that specifically covers drug therapy management to be maintained during the term, so a policy allowed to lapse or not renewed mid-term breaks the element while the agreement is still running.

timing_deadlines.event: A collaborative practice agreement relied on for the doctor of pharmacy route in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1.
timing_deadlines.consequence: The degree route is open only to a pharmacist who both earned a doctor of pharmacy degree and entered into a collaborative practice agreement on or before that date; for an agreement entered later the element must be met by five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist or under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)2.

forms_records.text: In the community pharmacy setting the supervising physician shall execute a written referral containing, at least, the patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis for which the services are authorized, the diagnosis of any comorbid conditions for which they are authorized, any known patient drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent, and any other specific instructions to the authorized pharmacist.
The list of contents for the community-pharmacy written referral is expressly not exhaustive, so satisfying every named item does not by itself close the question of what the referral should carry.

Individual referral and consent shall be recorded in the patient's record by the pharmacist and by the supervising physician; a single entry by either professional leaves the other's duty undischarged.
The referral itself must carry a diagnosis, because the supervising physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist.

243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient to the authorized pharmacist, and that written referral shall include a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions that are included in the collaborative drug therapy management.

role_duties.duty: Work within the four core verbs and the stated may-include limbs, satisfy the three laboratory conditions before ordering or evaluating a test, and stop short of any evaluation with a diagnostic component.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist proposing to enter an agreement
role_duties.duty: Satisfy the statutory elements in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's elements in 247 CMR 16.02(1): a current unrestricted licence in good standing together with current engagement in Massachusetts pharmacy practice, at least $1,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance maintained during the term and specifically covering drug therapy management, the credential element as 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) states it, the practice-focus element, and five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist as 243 CMR 2.12(1) defines the term
role_duties.duty: Be currently registered by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and in good standing, meet the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02, and participate in drug therapy management with a supervising physician pursuant to a written agreement with written protocols.

role_duties.role: Medical staff executive committee of a licensed hospital, or its designee
role_duties.duty: Approve collaborative drug therapy management before it is practised in that hospital.

role_duties.role: Medical director of a long-term care facility or of a hospice, or a designee
role_duties.duty: Approve collaborative drug therapy management in that facility or hospice setting.

role_duties.role: Attending physician in an ambulatory care clinic
role_duties.duty: Provide on-site supervision alongside the collaborating pharmacist, in addition to the clinic's approval of the arrangement.

role_duties.role: Physician or physician group as employer
role_duties.duty: May hire pharmacists for the purpose of practising collaborative drug therapy management under an agreement for the benefit of a patient of that physician or group.

role_duties.role: Retail or community pharmacy as employer
role_duties.duty: May engage a physician or licensed medical practitioner to conduct quality assurance reviews of its collaborating pharmacists, but may not employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement.
Assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist, and record the individual referral and consent in the patient's record.

role_duties.role: Supervising physician in a community pharmacy collaboration
role_duties.duty: Execute a written referral carrying the contents listed in 243 CMR 2.12(1), rather than relying on a consultation with the pharmacist.

May require a physician to give written notification to each authorized pharmacist with whom the physician is in an agreement where it enters a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice, summarily suspends a licence, or takes final disciplinary action, and may revoke the right to participate on any ground for discipline in 243 CMR 1.03(5).

Hold an active licence to practise medicine issued by the Board and be actively engaged in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field in which the collaborative management is to take place; act as the supervisor in the agreement, retaining the ultimate responsibility for the care of the patient; and assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management.

common_traps.text: Reading the laboratory limb as free-standing. It is conditioned on physician supervision or direct consultation and on approved protocols applicable to the practice setting, unlike the history and vital-signs limbs beside it.
Treating a diagnostic conclusion as permissible because the underlying test was properly ordered. The definition forbids a diagnostic component in the evaluation whatever the pedigree of the order.

Reading the credential element off the statute and stopping there. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) state a doctor of pharmacy degree as an alternative to five years of experience, but 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) makes the degree route depend on a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, and 243 CMR 2.12(1) requires an authorized pharmacist to meet 247 CMR 16.02.

Forgetting that the licence element has a second half, and reading the first half as no more than a current licence. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(a) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(a) require a current unrestricted licence in good standing, and the pharmacist must also currently be engaged in pharmacy practice in the commonwealth.

Answering an insurance question on the dollar figure alone. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(b) require $1,000,000 per occurrence, maintained during the term of the agreement, and cover that specifically reaches drug therapy management, so an aggregate-only or general-practice policy fails on the cover rather than on the amount.

Carrying the 0.5 continuing education unit alternative into 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e), which states five additional contact hours and no unit alternative, or describing the subject matter as collaborative practice agreements generally when both regulations tie it to the particular agreement.
Applying one approving body across all four settings, or treating a single system-wide approval as covering a hospital, a long-term care facility, a hospice and an ambulatory care clinic at once.
Overlooking the on-site supervision condition in an ambulatory care clinic, or treating it as an alternative to approval rather than an addition to it.
Assuming hospitals and ambulatory care clinics must be governed by different licensing provisions because they are listed separately; both are licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51.

Reading M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(e) as barring a pharmacy from employing any physician at all, when the bar attaches to the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement.
Treating a quality-assurance engagement as the prohibited purpose, or letting a job title decide the question when the subsection turns on what the physician is actually engaged to do.
Assuming an unrestricted medical licence keeps a collaboration alive. A controlled substances registration event alone deems the physician ineligible under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d).

Assuming the pharmacist will always be told before the authority lapses. Notification under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(e) is something the Board may require on the events it lists, and a controlled substances registration event is not among them.

Treating a person who asks for collaborative management, or who reports that a physician mentioned it, as a patient within the definition. The referral has to come from the supervising physician and carry a diagnosis.
Assuming the physician's chart entry discharges the recording duty, when individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record.
Assuming notice and consent are required in every setting rather than in the retail drug business setting named by the definition of patient.

Applying the community-pharmacy written referral formalities in a hospital, long-term care facility, hospice or ambulatory care clinic, where a consultation of the supervising physician and the authorized pharmacist about the patient is itself the referral.

Accepting a signed and detailed community-pharmacy referral that omits any known patient drug allergies or the statement that the patient has executed a written consent; both are named items in 243 CMR 2.12(1).

Treating a physician as eligible because nothing in 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) disqualifies him. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a) states a positive requirement: an active licence issued by the Board and active engagement in the clinical practice of medicine and patient care in the particular field of the collaboration.

Reading the setting-sensitive definition of Referral as the whole of the physician's paperwork. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) separately requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions, and does not confine that duty to the community pharmacy setting.
